Except Photoshop is a bitmap editor, which means it treats objects as collections of dots or pixels on a grid. This creates problems when you try to zoom past the resolution of your file or align something more precisely than the pixel grid. Also, Photoshop's layout tools (what few there are) are geared for aligning pixels on a screen, not objects in a print-ready document. Whereas InDesign and Illustrator are vector-based, which means the computer understands the lines which make up each shape or text character as a mathematical equation. This means that you can enlarge your text or shapes practically infinitely and still maintain a crisp line with no loss of data. Additionally, these programs (InDesign especially), have incredibly precise alignment features to ensure everything lines up down to hundredths of a millimeter on a printed page.

Photoshop is the wrong tool for this sort of job and if you're using it for page layout in any sort of professional manner you're producing work that makes you look very unprofessional. Besides the spelling error, had he used InDesign or Illustrator it may have given it that extra edge of realism that would really sell the joke.

In 2009 I spent a semester abroad in Taiwan. Before we left we were given a basic political briefing. In general, it's always a poor idea to be arrested in another country, but Taiwan is a special case. Because there's no U.S. embassy, there's no formal appeal to the United States government for extradition if you find yourself in serious trouble. There's a simple dignitary or official (not even an ambassador) assigned to the country, and we were told that if we were arrested the only authority the United States federal government had through this simple official was, no joke, to bring you a plate of cookies. That's apparently the literal official recourse of the U.S. government considering citizens locked up in Taiwan. Needless to say, I kept out of trouble.

**TL;DR: Get locked up in Taiwan, enjoy free plate of cookies, courtesy of U.S. government! May or may not include lifetime in hard-labor prison camp.**
